newsitem.title: USA: United Airlines, city compromise on benefits.
newsitem.headline: United Airlines, city compromise on benefits.

text.p: United Airlines and San Francisco's city government have reached a compromise that should end a dispute over whether the airline must offer benefits to unmarried life partners of its employees, officials said on Saturday.

San Francisco's governing Board of Supervisors had delayed approving a 25-year lease UAL Corp's United Airlines was seeking for a flight kitchen and equipment repair facility at San Francisco International Airport.

The supervisors wanted the company to comply with a city ordinance passed late last year that requires companies doing business with San Francisco to provide the same benefits they provide to spouses to employees' unmarried partners, whether gay or heterosexual. The law covers benefits such as bereavement leave, medical leave and health insurance.

The airline objected, saying the new law does not take effect until June and that the condition had not been mentioned during negotiations on the lease last year, news reports said. Another issue was whether companies must offer the benefits nationwide or worldwide, not just in the city.
City officials and United Airlines said a proposed agreement had been reached, which is expected to be voted on by the city's Board of Supervisors Monday.

Supervisor Tom Ammiano, who introduced the domestic partners law, said the proposed agreement consisted of a two-year lease plus a 23-year option. To qualify for the option, United would have to comply with the domestic partners law, he said.
According to Ammiano, United has committed to complying with the domestic partners law in the future.

"They are going to go for a two-year contract on the kitchen. In the language of that lease ... is a commitment to full compliance with the domestic partner ordinance particularly based on the 23-year renewal of that lease that they absolutely need," said Ammiano.

After June, when the city law takes effect, United would be applying for several other contracts at San Francisco International Airport and would have to comply with the law, Ammiano said. "So therefore the issue becomes moot," he told a news conference outside a United ticket office.
United Airlines, the biggest carrier at San Francisco airport, does not currently extend benefits to domestic partners in the United States.
Company spokesman Tony Molinaro confirmed there was an agreement that would go before the Board of Supervisors, but he declined to give any details.
Molinaro said United felt the city ordinance could "create an issue around the country and around the world." "We're looking at it very closely from financial and legal aspects."
"We feel like we need a little time to look at the ordinance and figure out the issues it raises," he said.

David Tomb, founder of "United at United", an association of gay and lesbian employees at United Airlines, hailed the agreement, saying: "We're really claiming today as a victory for not only gay and lesbian employees but a victory for ... non-discrimination."
